## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}
This is a direct implementation of a matrix in mathematics @sec-matrix.
That is a rectangular object that contains rows and columns.
If four different persons bought three fruits of different quantity, then one can create a matrix with three rows and four columns to store the data
ADD a matrix
or a matrix of four rows and three columns to store the data.
ADD the transposed matrix.

Notice that there is no chapter on vector in basic mathematics, that is because, mathematically, a vector is simply a "one dimensional" matrix.

Reusing the analogy of stacked aparment as a vector, the matrix allows for more apartments in each floor. So an apartment is now identified by the floor number and the order in that floor. And similar to a vector, a matrix needs to be homogeneous.
In general, a matrix object it is better used for mathematical computation.

In many cases, the data could be heterogeneous, in that case we could use data frame @sec-dataframe or @sec-list.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
To construct a matrix, we need the informations: the size of the matrix: how many rows (nrow) and columns (ncol), the list of all the elements in a form of vectors so we need a vector of length nrow x ncol, and a way to indicate how to arrange the elements.

In R, to contruct a matrix we use matrix(), matrix_name <- matrix(data, nrow, ncol, byrow).
Most of the time, ncol is not because it is inferred from length of data divided by nrow.
byrow is argument that takes boolean telling whether it should be arranged by rows or by colums. The default is

See function @sec-functionCoding for

To access element, we use the same [] as in vector but with two dimensions [row position, column position].
Be aware that the first is vertical (as in floor number and the second is horizontal, and the order in that floor).

- matrix_name[1, 2] means to retrive the element in the first row (horizontal) and second column
- matrix_name[3, ] (leaving the second dimension empty) means taking the third row
- matrix[, 3] (leaving the first dimension empty) means taking the third column (see the output below)
- matrix [ -2 , -3] the negative means remove that specific column, or row, or both matrix []
